seo.title: Karmic tail 15 11 5 compatibility: The Devil, Strength, The Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 11 5 compatibility: The Devil, Strength and The Hierophant in a couple's matrix, read through Beauty and the Beast, with a worked example.

title: Karmic tail 15-11-5 in compatibility: the secret of Beauty and the Beast
short: In the first printed Beauty and the Beast (1740) the Beast asks the same question every evening: will Beauty let him sleep with her. Sixteen years later the governess Leprince de Beaumont retold the tale for her pupils and rewrote the question: "Beauty, will you be my wife?" The couple's karmic tail 15-11-5 is the road between those two questions: from a desire that holds two people like a chain, through the long taming of fear, to the word, the marriage and the families before whom the union has to be named.

paragraphs: Most people know Beauty and the Beast from the cartoon, and the cartoon grew out of Beaumont's retelling. But the first to write it was Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve: in 1740 she placed a long, almost novel-length story in her collection La Jeune Américaine et les contes marins (The Young American and Sea Tales). In Villeneuve, after supper the Beast bluntly asks Beauty whether she will let him sleep with her. The first time she cries out: "Ah, heaven! I am lost." After that the question comes every evening, and the author simply calls it "the usual question".

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont, a Frenchwoman working as a governess in England, abridged the tale in 1756 for her Magasin des enfants, known in English as The Young Misses Magazine. It is a textbook written as conversations between a wise governess and her pupils: geography, history, Scripture, and fairy tales in between. Here the Beast's question is different: "Beauty, will you be my wife?" — "No, Beast!" For three months it is asked every evening at nine o'clock. In 1761 the book was translated into Russian as Detskoe uchilishche, "The Children's School, or Moral Conversations between a Wise Teacher and Her Noble Pupils of Various Ages".

The third version is Russian. As a child, Sergei Aksakov heard the tale "not once but dozens of times" from the housekeeper Pelageya. As a schoolboy, lying in the school infirmary, he borrowed Detskoe uchilishche, reached "Beauty and the Beast" and, in his words, recognised his own Alenky tsvetochek (The Scarlet Flower) "from the first lines". He wrote it down in old age and published it in 1858 as an appendix to The Childhood Years of Bagrov the Grandson. In Aksakov there is no question at all: until the last page the monster says nothing of marriage and speaks to the merchant's daughter in letters of fire on a marble wall.

The three versions take the tail apart. In Villeneuve the entry sounds loudest — bodily desire. In Aksakov the middle takes up most of the room — getting used to each other. In Beaumont everything comes down to the main task — the question of marriage and a lesson in what a husband should be.

sections.h2: A curse written in the order of the cards
paragraphs: The strangest clue lies in the second half of Villeneuve's novel, which almost nobody reads. There the prince tells how he became the Beast. He was raised by a fairy protector. When he grew up she demanded his hand, and he refused: "I do not want to lose my freedom so soon." The fairy struck him on the head, and his hands became paws. This is the curse she laid on him (our translation):

"I order you to appear as stupid as you are hideous, and to wait in this state until a young and beautiful girl comes to find you of her own free will, though she is convinced you will devour her. It is also necessary that, once she no longer fears for her life, she grows fond enough of you to propose marriage to you herself."

The sentence holds three conditions, and they come in the order of the tail 15-11-5. To come of one's own will to the place where ruin waits is The Devil, a voluntary captivity. To stop being afraid is Strength: both Waite and Wen see in it a mastery not over an outer beast, but over passions and fear. To propose marriage herself is The Hierophant, a union sealed by a word.

At parting the fairy added a fourth rule: "you must forget who you are. If you let yourself be flattered by empty honours or grand titles, you are lost." This is The Hierophant too, only in its minus: ranks, status, other people's approval.

So the Beast's story begins with a marriage demanded by an older woman with power over him, and ends with a marriage proposed of free will. Both bonds belong to the fifth card. Between them stand a palace where everything is given at once and long evenings in which people learn to be less afraid.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a palace where every wish comes true
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the entry M is what the couple strives for together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. With The Devil at the entry, a couple enters its task through a strong bond: "I want everything, and now", "you are mine", "I will never let you go".

The Beast's palace works exactly like this. In Aksakov the merchant merely thinks, "All very fine, but there is nothing to eat" (Aksakov is quoted here in our translation) — and a laid table rises before him. He wants to sleep — and a bed of pure gold appears. To the daughter the monster writes on the wall: "whatever you wish, whatever comes into your mind, I will gladly do." Wen puts it plainly: The Devil is "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification". The palace grants a wish before anyone has managed to say it aloud.

For couples with this tail the beginning is often like that palace. Messages until three in the morning, presents nobody asked for, each other's keys within a month. It feels as if the other person guesses what one wants, so words can be saved. The danger is right there: a wish that is never spoken stays unknown, and later turns into resentment. Among the tasks of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya names silence about one's own wishes and attempts to hold a partner through closeness, money or status. The palace feeds, dresses, entertains — and holds.

In Aksakov the entry to the task is framed as a bargain. The merchant picked the flower without asking, so he owes a debt. The monster demands "your honest merchant's word and a pledge in your own hand": to send one of his daughters in his place. And at once he sets a condition that breaks the whole contract: "I want no bondmaid: let your daughter come here out of love for you, of her own will and wish." A captivity one can only enter of one's own will is exactly The Devil at the entry to a couple's tail. The bond begins as a chain, but people put this chain on themselves.

The first letters of fire on the wall speak the language of this card turned inside out: "I am not your master but your obedient slave. You are my mistress." Master and slave is The Devil's vocabulary, only here the stronger one calls himself the slave. In a couple this vocabulary can be tender and can be heavy: "I'm all yours", "you'd be nowhere without me", "I gave up everything for you". While it is tender, it looks like love. Once it turns into a tally, it becomes a chain.

In its plus, The Devil at the entry holds the couple's deepest wish: to be accepted together with one's beast. Each brings into the union something they themselves find unsightly: a quick temper, a past nobody mentions, a fear of poverty, a habit of vanishing for a day. In the plus of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya writes of couples who accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes. The condition is the same in all three tales: to love "in the shape of a monster".

And one detail from outside the tale. Pelageya, from whom Aksakov heard The Scarlet Flower, ran away from her former masters to Astrakhan with her father when she was very young and lived there for more than twenty years. On learning that she had "passed" to Aksakov's grandfather, she came back from her flight of her own accord. The grandfather, Aksakov writes, received her kindly "out of respect for so voluntary a return". The tale of a voluntary captivity was told by a woman who had chosen to come back herself. The question at the entry to this tail is not "is there passion" but what in this bond is free will and what is a chain.

The numbers add their own clue: neither partner brings The Devil into the couple. The couple's entry is the sum of the entries of the partners' personal tails, and there one partner has The Hanged Man and the other The Empress (63% of such couples), or one has The Lovers and the other The Hermit (37%). Neither personal tail contains a fifteen, as with other couples who have The Devil at the entry. The palace appears only when the two meet.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: letters of fire, a voice, twilight
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle N no meaning of its own; it is an "addition" to the main task. We read it as the road: what the couple does to get from the entry to the main task. In this tail the road is Strength.

In Aksakov the taming goes step by step, and no step can be skipped. At first there are only letters of fire. Then a voice — "loud, rough and hoarse", and even then the monster speaks "in an undertone". The merchant's daughter "shuddered at first", but "mastered her fear and did not let it show that she was frightened". Then she asks him to show himself. He agrees only to twilight, when the sun has set behind the forest, and passes at a distance, across the path. She screams and falls senseless. Coming round, she hears someone weeping beside her: "You have destroyed me, my beloved beauty." And then "she mastered her great fear".

Wen opens her reading of Strength in almost the same words: "The Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears." And further: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." So it is in the tale: the monster never once raises a paw against her. It is not he who is tamed. What is tamed is fear: hers of his face, his of her leaving.

Both need Strength, and in the Beast it is even more visible. In Beaumont he asks his question every evening for three months and every evening hears "no". In Villeneuve Beauty notes that the Beast "does not persist in his requests and shows no resentment at my refusals". When the prince later complains to the fairy that Beauty will never accept such a proposal, the fairy answers only: "Patience, perseverance, or all is lost." This is Strength in the old sense: fortitude. To ask and hear "no" without revenge is the central skill of the middle of this tail.

Waite's list of meanings for Strength includes the word "magnanimity". In the tale it takes the shape of a ring under the pillow. Agreeing to show himself, the monster says: "I do not want your bondage and endless torment: in your bedchamber, under your pillow, you will find my golden ring." He himself leaves her the key to the way out. The Devil's chain holds; Strength leaves the chance to leave, and that is why the person stays.

In a couple's life the middle of the task looks ordinary. One day a roar breaks through: one partner snaps after a hard day, the other wants to "fall senseless" — slam the door, go back to their mother, go silent for a week. Strength means staying and saying: "I'm frightened when you shout." And for the other, learning to speak in an undertone. Among the tasks of the eleventh energy Lisovskaya names what takes months in the tale: saying from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, and showing feelings openly. In the minus she has the struggle for leadership and inflated demands on a partner's looks and status. The last sounds almost like a retelling of the tale: "put on something decent, you don't come to my family dressed like that."

There is also the opposite minus: mistaking for taming a patience that silently stores up fear. Beauty and the Beast is not a manual for endurance. In all three versions the Beast does not touch her and hands over the ring himself. If someone in a couple fears for their safety, if there are threats or violence, this is not a story about taming: help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

The numbers say two things about the middle. Strength in the middle of a couple's tail is always assembled from two other cards — from the middles of the personal tails. In 63% of such couples these are The Tower and The Fool: a collapse and a step into the unknown. That is how the tale begins: in Beaumont the merchant loses his fortune at a stroke, and the daughter goes of her own accord to a place nobody expects to return from. The second thing is more surprising. In the same 63% Strength already stands in the centre of one partner's personal chart, while the other has Justice in the centre — the very two cards that Waite swapped. Together they give The Sun in the centre of the couple.

sections.h2: Main task: the word, the sisters and the clocks set back an hour
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the main task D is read mostly through its minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. With The Hierophant this means family, custom, rule and the word once given. In all three versions the danger at the end comes not from the beast but from the relatives, and the relatives have one weapon — time and the word.

In Aksakov the daughter is allowed home for three days and three nights. Her father blesses her, and it is agreed that she will leave an hour before the deadline. "It vexed" the elder sisters: they "set every clock in the house back a full hour". When the true hour comes, her heart "began to ache and wring", while the sisters ask her "about this and that" and hold her back. She puts on the ring by the slow clocks and, appearing in the palace, cries out that she has returned "a whole hour and a minute before the appointed time". The monster lies on the hillock, his paws around the scarlet flower, "lifeless".

In Beaumont Beauty promises to return in eight days. The sisters plot to keep her longer: "Her stupid Beast will fly into a rage when he finds she has broken her word, and will very likely devour her." They tear their hair, feigning grief, and she promises to remain another eight days. In Villeneuve the spell is already broken and the beast is gone — and then the prince's mother enters the hall. On learning who the bride is, the queen steps back two paces: "What! You are only a merchant's daughter!" — and calls such a marriage "an alliance so shameful for us". The beast has vanished; the relatives remain.

For a couple with this tail, the sisters with the clocks rarely look like villains. A mother rings on Saturday morning: "You are coming, aren't you? At least till the evening." The evening becomes a night, the night becomes a week "all together as a family". The parents have a key to the flat they helped pay for, and they come when it suits them. A sister discusses what the partner is wearing; one of the parents explains how the renovation ought to be done. No clock is ever set back more than an hour, but hour by hour the couple is late for itself. For Lisovskaya the tasks of the fifth energy in a couple are almost all about the same thing: parents, relatives, the partner's family. In the tale all of it fits into one scene with the clocks.

The way out is not to break with the family. Aksakov's daughter leaves each time with her father's blessing, and at the end "the honest merchant gave his blessing". The task is subtler: the two of them set the deadline, and the word they have given each other weighs more than other people's clocks. Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fifth energy to get on with the relatives without letting them inside the couple's borders, and to create holidays and places of their own.

The second half of the task is to name the union. Begging the monster to show himself, Aksakov's heroine tries every name of kinship: "If you are an old man, be a grandfather to me; if middle-aged, be an uncle to me; if you are young, be my sworn brother; and as long as I live, be my heart's friend." Any name will do except one. Only the last one breaks the spell: "Rise, wake up, my heart's friend, I love you as my desired bridegroom!" The condition of the curse, as the prince explains afterwards, is that a girl should love him in the shape of a monster "and wish to be my lawful wife". In Beaumont the same thing is said as a vow: "Here and now I offer you my hand, and swear that I will marry none but you."

In the two words "desired bridegroom" both ends of the tail meet. "Desired" comes from the entry, from The Devil. "Bridegroom" comes from the main task, from The Hierophant. Waite calls The Hierophant "the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature". Aksakov's monster is a "beast of the forest, wonder of the sea", nature itself, forest and sea. The main task is to bring him into the world of institution: to say aloud, in front of people, who he is. For a modern couple this is our reading, and it need not mean a wedding. The Hierophant asks for a name and a form: who we are to each other, what we promise, which rules in this home are ours. Couples with this tail can live for years as "heart's friends" — together but without a name, while the relatives call the partner "that one of yours".

The form itself has a minus too. Villeneuve's queen measures the union by rank, and the fairy has to reveal that Beauty is in fact a king's daughter. Aksakov's curse cancels this in advance: the maiden may be "of whatever birth and rank she might be". The law is needed; rank is not. And Beaumont shows another temptation of the fifth card — the lesson. "It is neither good looks nor brains in a husband that make a woman happy; it is beauty of character, virtue, kindness," Beauty reasons. Wen writes that "The Hierophant is about the pedagogy of wisdom". A couple with this tail would do well to watch that the union does not become a school where one teaches the other how to be.

And the last thing. The disenchanted prince in Aksakov says: "You loved me in the shape of a hideous monster… now love me in human shape." The good fairy in Beaumont, handing Beauty a crown, adds: "I hope that the pomp of royalty will not destroy your virtues." The Hierophant's task does not end with the vow; it begins with it: to love an ordinary person in an everyday home, without the palace and the letters of fire.

Here too the numbers have left a trace. The couple's main task is the sum of the partners' personal karmic tasks, and in 63% of such couples these are The Emperor and The Sun. Our reading: in the main task the order of the father's house meets a new life — the merchant and his youngest, best-loved daughter.
In its minus the tail runs in a circle, and each turn shows its own card.

ol: Desire binds quickly. A palace where everything comes true without words, and silence about what one really wants (15).
The beast shows itself: a temper, jealousy, the past. One partner tries to tame by force — control and conditions — the other falls senseless: goes silent, leaves (11 in its minus).
To decide who is right, the couple calls in rules from outside: "normal people don't do this", "let's ask Mum" (5 in its minus).

The relatives take a side and set the clocks back. The two make up where they began — in the palace: with closeness, with a present, without words. Nothing has been named, and the circle starts again.

paragraphs: The price of such a circle is years spent between honeymoon and quarrel, without a name or rules of their own. Every dispute is decided by other people's clocks, and the wishes are never said aloud.

sections.h2: The Sun in the centre: why the Beast comes at twilight
paragraphs: In 71.4% of couples with the tail 15-11-5 The Sun stands in the centre of the matrix. In a personal matrix The Sun never falls in the centre, for any date of birth: this card appears in the centre only for a couple. The centre is "The atmosphere inside the couple", what lies between two people when nobody is watching.

In the tale the Beast lives at twilight. In Aksakov he shows himself only "when the red sun sets behind the forest". In Beaumont he comes at nine in the evening. In Villeneuve the real prince visits Beauty only in her dreams. And at the very moment Beaumont's vow is spoken, the castle suddenly becomes "ablaze with lights". The tale moves from twilight to light, and the couple's centre stands where the tale ends. Our reading: inside such a couple the beast finds it hard to hide in the half-dark for long. A sunlit atmosphere makes everything visible, and the beast has to be met in daylight, not at dusk.

In the remaining 28.6% the centre holds The Wheel of Fortune: fate that turns. Beaumont's tale also begins with a turn of the wheel — the merchant loses his fortune at a stroke, and later carries a chest of gold away from the palace.

"The couple's values" in such couples are most often The Empress (55.6%), less often The Hanged Man (25.4%) and The World (19%). The Empress is a garden where things grow if they are tended. The scarlet flower grows in a garden on a hillock, and it is there that the merchant's daughter finds the monster for the last time. The Hanged Man recalls the very first turn of the plot: the daughter goes to the beast "in his stead", taking on another's fate of her own free will.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: a beast above people, a woman with a beast, people without a beast
paragraphs: On Waite's card of The Devil a horned figure stands on an altar, and chains run from a ring on the altar to the necks of a man and a woman. The chained figures have tails, "to signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces". Of the one exalted above them Waite writes that he "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman" — like the monster who writes on the wall that he is a slave. And tails beneath human faces are the Beast of the tale: an animal body and a human mind that he is forbidden to show. In Beaumont the wicked fairy "forbade me to betray any sign of intelligence"; in Villeneuve she ordered him "to appear as stupid as you are hideous". That is why the Beast's question in Villeneuve is so crude. Later the prince admits that he spoke in words the fairy had "chosen on purpose to be low and childish".

On the card of Strength (VIII for Waite, 11 in the matrix) a woman is closing a lion's jaws, and the lion follows her on a chain of flowers. For Waite, "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion": the picture shows not a fight but what comes after it. He explains: "There is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions, and she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation." The beast is still in the picture, but it is no longer above people; it is beside a human being.

On the card of The Hierophant there is no beast. The high priest sits between pillars, crossed keys at his feet, two ministers kneeling before him. The three cards of the tail show where the beast goes: first it is above people, then beside a woman, then it is gone. In the tale it vanishes at the very moment the vow is spoken.

sections.h2: Worked example: the couple's tail for 09.05.1976 and 14.04.1975
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. First the personal tails are calculated.
The year is reduced by adding its digits: 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5, and 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Now the couple's tail:

This is the most common version of the tail: the personal tails 12-16-4 and 3-22-19 produce it in 63% of cases. One partner has Strength in the centre and the other Justice, so the couple's centre is 11 + 8 = 19, The Sun. "The couple's values" here are The Hanged Man, 12.

This couple has a rare detail. The Hierophant stands not only in the main task but also in the spheres "How others see the couple" (9 + 14 = 23 → 5) and "What fills the union" (14 + 18 = 32 → 5). Three or more fives occur in only 3% of couples with this tail. Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. The sum gives The Devil again — the card of the entry. Anyone who likes such coincidences will see the whole tale in them: marriage, custom and family, added together, lead back to the desire where it all began.

sections.h2: Why 15-11-5 is never a personal tail
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task. From 15 and 5 that would give 20, the tail 15-20-5 with Judgement in the middle. In a couple the middle is not recalculated: it is added up from the middles of the partners' personal tails, and the result is 11. So 15-11-5 exists only for a couple, and the Strength in its middle is something no single person carries in their own tail.

No other couple's tails are made of the same three numbers: the calculation never produces the permutations 5-11-15 or 11-15-5. If Lisovskaya's book or another calculator shows 5-11-15, it is the same tail written in reverse order, from the main task to the entry.

sections.h2: The strong version: a ring on one's own finger
paragraphs: In the strong version of the tail all three cards remain, but they change sign. The Devil becomes attachment in the good sense: the two know each other's dark sides and do not turn them into weapons. Strength becomes the ability to hold without a chain. The Hierophant becomes a union with its own rules, where the relatives are loved but only the owners of the house set its clocks.
What helps a couple through this tail:

ul: say wishes aloud instead of waiting for the palace to guess;
ask, and hear "no" without punishment — the Beast heard it for three months;
leave each other a "ring under the pillow": the right to go to one's family and come back;
set the deadlines with relatives together and keep the word once given, even if someone's clocks run slow;
do not turn the union into a school: no lecturing, no remaking each other;
name the union in one's own words: who we are to each other and what we promise.

paragraphs: In the tale it is she who speaks the last word, but in a couple with this tail the roles are not divided by sex. Each of the two, on some evening, is the Beast who asks and the Beauty who decides whether to say "yes".

Aksakov's ring works on one condition only: "whoever puts it on the little finger of the right hand will find himself wherever he wishes." It is not put on someone else; it is put on oneself. That is the difference between a chain and a vow. A chain is put on another person. A ring a person puts on themselves, and it leads to the place they have chosen to return to.

ul: **15 — The Devil, "Entry to the task".** Where the couple starts and what it wants together: to be everything to each other, to have it all at once, to belong. This is its common language and its first resistance.

**11 — Strength, "Middle of the task".** What the couple goes through: taming. Not chaining the "beast" and not running from it, but learning to stay close to fear, anger and jealousy — one's own and the other's.

**5 — The Hierophant, "Main task".** What the couple has to learn: to turn a bond into a union with its own word and its own rules, with parents, relatives, customs and other people's clocks all around.

intro: The secret of this tail is hidden in the tale itself. The spell is broken not by a kiss and not by beauty, but by one word spoken of one's own free will. The Devil's chain and The Hierophant's vow bind two people equally tightly. The difference between them is settled in the middle, on the card of Strength: is a person being held, or do they stay of their own accord.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-11-5 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix, the main line of its tasks. **At the entry stands The Devil**: the couple begins with a strong desire and attachment, which can become both a common language and a chain. **In the middle stands Strength**: the road leads through taming fear, anger and jealousy without brute force. **The main task is The Hierophant**: to build a union with its own word and rules and to keep its borders in the face of relatives and other people's customs.

No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict, and the method gives no compatibility percentages. The Devil at the entry does not mean addiction or violence: it is a theme of desire and freedom that the couple works through together. In their strong version the same three cards describe a deep attachment, the ability to hold without a chain, and a union with rules of its own.

faq.q: Is the tail 5-11-15 the same tail?
faq.a: Yes, it is the same tail written in reverse order. On the site a couple's tail is read from the entry to the main task — M, N, D — while Lisovskaya writes it in her book from the main task: D, D2, D1. No other couple's tails are made of the numbers 15, 11 and 5.

faq.q: Does the 15-11-5 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task, and 15 and 5 would give the tail 15-20-5. In a couple the middle is added up from the middles of the two personal tails, so Strength in the middle is possible only for a couple.

faq.q: How common is the couple's tail 15-11-5?
faq.a: About one couple in 208 has it, which is 0.481% of all couples and 55th place among the 97 couple's tails. Most often it is formed by the personal tails 12-16-4 and 3-22-19 (63% of such couples), less often by 6-8-20 and 9-3-21 (28%), 6-20-14 and 9-9-18 (9%), and 6-20-14 and 9-18-9 (1%).

And at once the monster sets a condition that breaks the whole contract: "I want no bondmaid: let your daughter come here out of love for you, of her own will and wish." **The bond begins as a chain, but people put this chain on themselves.** The first letters of fire on the wall speak The Devil's language turned inside out: "I am not your master but your obedient slave." In a couple this vocabulary can be tender — "I'm all yours" — and it can be heavy — "I gave up everything for you". Once it turns into a tally, it becomes a chain.

In its plus, The Devil at the entry holds the couple's deepest wish: for a person to be accepted together with their beast — a quick temper, a past nobody mentions, a fear of poverty. The condition is the same in every version of the tale: to love "in the shape of a monster".

report.h3: It is fear that gets tamed, not the beast

report: In Aksakov the taming goes step by step: first letters of fire, then a voice, "loud, rough and hoarse", then a meeting at twilight, when the sun has set behind the forest. The merchant's daughter screams and falls senseless, and on coming round she hears someone weeping beside her. And then "she mastered her great fear". Wen writes about Strength in almost the same words: "The Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears." The monster never once raises a paw against her. It is not he who is tamed but fear: hers of his face, his of her leaving.

In Beaumont the Beast asks his question every evening for three months and every evening hears "no". When the prince in Villeneuve complains to the fairy that Beauty will never accept such a proposal, the fairy answers only: "Patience, perseverance, or all is lost." **To ask and hear "no" without revenge is the central skill of the middle of this tail.** And the "magnanimity" that Waite lists among the meanings of Strength takes the shape of a ring under the pillow in the tale: the monster himself leaves her the key to the way out. A chain holds; Strength leaves the chance to leave, and that is why the person stays.

Beauty and the Beast is not a manual for endurance: in every version the Beast does not touch her and hands over the ring himself. If someone in a couple fears for their safety, if there are threats or violence, help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

report.h3: The sisters set back the clocks

report: The main task is read mostly through its minus, and at the end of the tale the danger comes not from the beast but from the relatives. In Aksakov the elder sisters "set every clock in the house back a full hour", and the heroine returns to the palace sure that she is in time — and the monster lies "lifeless". In Beaumont the sisters hold Beauty back so that she breaks her word. In Villeneuve the spell is already broken, and the prince's mother steps back two paces: the bride is "only a merchant's daughter". The beast has vanished; the relatives remain.

For a couple with this tail, the sisters with the clocks rarely look like villains: "at least till the evening", the evening becomes a night, the night becomes a week "all together as a family". No clock is ever set back more than an hour, but hour by hour the couple is late for itself. The way out is not a break with the family — Aksakov's daughter leaves each time with her father's blessing. **The two of them set the deadline, and the word they have given each other weighs more than other people's clocks.**

report.h3: The spell is broken by a word

report: Aksakov's heroine tries every name of kinship for the monster: "be a grandfather to me", "be an uncle to me", "be my sworn brother", "be my heart's friend". Only the last word breaks the spell: "I love you as my desired bridegroom!" In those two words both ends of the tail meet: "desired" comes from The Devil, "bridegroom" from The Hierophant. The main task is to name the union: who we are to each other, what we promise, which rules in this home are ours. And to remember the words of the disenchanted prince: "now love me in human shape" — without the palace and the letters of fire.

Aksakov's ring works on one condition: "whoever puts it on the little finger of the right hand will find himself wherever he wishes." **A chain is put on another person. A ring a person puts on themselves**, and it leads to the place they have chosen to return to.
